694.title: Magha Puja, deeper
694.hook: the verses taught that day: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind (Dhammapada 183–185)
694.howItsDone: On Magha Puja, Theravada Buddhists in Thailand, Laos and Cambodia visit temples, keep precepts, listen to teachings and walk three times around a shrine at dusk carrying candles, incense and flowers; the Ovada Patimokkha verses are often chanted.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Losar, the Tibetan new year, and your line, a fresh year. Did you clean your corner, and let something old be over? Today, a full moon in Thailand. Day six hundred ninety-four.

Sabbapapassa akaranam. On a full-moon night in Thailand, Laos or Cambodia, those Pali words may be chanted in a temple hall, the opening of a short verse. In year one you met the night it remembers: the commentaries tell of twelve hundred and fifty monks who came to the Bamboo Grove near Rajagaha without being called, and of the Buddha giving them the whole teaching in three short verses. You also met the first of those verses. Today we stay with all three, and with what the Long Discourses add about who speaks them. Today: Magha Puja, deeper.
screen: `SABBAPAPASSA AKARANAM.` → `THE NIGHT, REMEMBERED.` → `NOW, ALL THREE VERSES.`

segments.voice: The three verses are known as the Ovada Patimokkha, the exhortation. The Dhammapada keeps them as verses 183 to 185. Here's the first, in Max Müller's translation: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." Look at the middle phrase. The Pali word Müller renders as good is kusala, which other translators give as skillful or wholesome. So the second move is more than being nice. It's taking up, on purpose, what actually helps. The second verse, paraphrased, calls patience the highest austerity, and nirvana the highest thing of all. Then it adds: someone who strikes or insults others isn't a true renunciant, however they dress. Patience sits where a reader might expect fasting or hardship. The third verse turns it all into a short list: don't blame, don't strike, live restrained by the training, be moderate in food, sit and sleep in a quiet place, and give yourself to the higher mind. Notice that the list begins with harm and ends with the mind, just as the first verse does. Now the detail from the Long Discourses. In the Mahapadana Sutta, Digha Nikaya 14, the Buddha tells of Vipassi, a Buddha of an age long past, gathering his monks and reciting these same verses. So the first verse's phrase, the teaching of all the Awakened, is taken at its word: in that telling, this is what Buddhas say. Not one teacher's slogan. A shared refrain. Some teachers read the three moves as a ladder: restraint, then goodness, then a clear mind. Others read them as one movement, happening together. The verses themselves just set them side by side, short enough to chant in a breath, and the tradition hears in them the heart of it.
screen: `KUSALA: GOOD, OR SKILLFUL.` · `PATIENCE, THE HIGHEST AUSTERITY.` · `A SHORT LIST FOR A LIFE.` · `A PAST BUDDHA SAYS IT TOO.` · then, large: `THE HEART OF IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do all three today. Start now, sitting. That's the third one: clear the mind. Just follow the breath in and out, and let the water settle. Then, before the bell, choose the other two. One harm you'll hold back from today: a sharp word, a careless habit. And one good thing you'll actually do: a call, a gift, a hand. Hold both in mind, simply, and come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Magha Puja. The full-moon day remembering the gathering of the twelve hundred and fifty, and the verses: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind. Today's word.
Your line: the heart of it. Tonight, before sleep, check all three: what harm did you skip, what good did you do, and when did your mind clear? Day six hundred ninety-four.

pairs: monks who came without being called

myth: kusala, in 'to do good', can only be translated as good
other translators give it as skillful or wholesome.
the Long Discourses tell of a past Buddha reciting these verses

the second verse calls patience the highest austerity

fork.setup: you are Vipassi, a Buddha of an age long past, and your monks have gathered before you. what do you give them?
options: a new teaching no one has heard before.
the same short verses: patience, no harm, the good, a clear mind.
nothing; you sit with them in silence.
fork.reveal: in Digha Nikaya 14 he recites these same verses. the teaching of all the Awakened is shared, not invented fresh.

original.note: Pali, the opening of Dhammapada 183: the not-doing of all evil.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism is mostly meditation.
what it means: the summary verse puts not harming and doing good first, then clearing the mind.
what a scholar hears: Ovada Patimokkha, the exhortation, distinct from the longer monastic rule recited each fortnight.

695.title: Saga Dawa
695.hook: the Tibetan month of the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing, when good deeds are said to multiply
695.tomorrow: Year two close: his own words
695.howItsDone: During Saga Dawa many Tibetan Buddhists walk pilgrim circuits such as the Lingkhor around Lhasa, give to beggars and monasteries, free animals, keep vegetarian, recite mantras and make offerings, especially on the full moon of Saga Dawa Duchen.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Magha Puja, and three short verses, and your line, the heart of it. Did you check all three last night: a harm skipped, a good done, a moment of clear mind? Day six hundred ninety-five.

The circuit around the old city of Lhasa is already full by sunrise. People walk it clockwise, spinning prayer wheels, murmuring mantras. Some stop every few steps to bow all the way to the ground. Along the route, people sit with open bowls, and pilgrims press small notes into bowl after bowl. It's not a single holy day, and it isn't only in Lhasa. It's a whole month. In Tibet, this is Saga Dawa.
screen: `A CIRCLE AROUND LHASA.` → `BOWLS ALONG THE ROUTE.` → `A WHOLE MONTH.`

segments.voice: Saga Dawa is the fourth month of the Tibetan calendar, usually falling around May or June. Dawa means month, or moon. Saga is the name of a star group, a lunar mansion the full moon sits near that month. So: the month of Saga. What makes it holy? In Tibetan tradition, the Buddha's birth, his awakening and his passing are all remembered in this month, with the big day on the full moon, called Saga Dawa Duchen, the great occasion. You may remember Vesak, where Theravada lands keep all three on one full moon. This is a Tibetan cousin of that same idea, with its own dates and customs: in Tibet, the birth is often marked on a different day, earlier in the month. Then comes the part people talk about most. Tibetan teachers say that during Saga Dawa, the effect of any action, good or harmful, is multiplied many times over. On the full moon, some say, by a hundred thousand. Some teachers put the stress on attention: a month when every small act is said to count for more, so people make them on purpose. They walk the pilgrim circuits, around the Jokhang, around Lhasa, and some walk all the way around Mount Kailash. Some families give up meat for the month. Some buy animals destined for slaughter and set them free. And they give, especially to anyone with a bowl out on the pilgrim route. Notice what that does to a month. A note pressed into a bowl, an animal bought back and set free, a day without meat: in Saga Dawa, each small act is treated as large.
screen: `DAWA, MONTH. SAGA, A STAR.` · `BIRTH, AWAKENING, PASSING.` · `GOOD DEEDS MULTIPLIED.` · `CIRCLES, FREED ANIMALS, GIFTS.` · then, large: `THE HOLY MONTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give generously this month. Sit, and settle into the breath. Now let three people or causes come to mind, one at a time. Someone near you who could use something. Someone you pass every day and never really see. A cause you've meant to help and haven't. Hold each one for a few breaths. Ask quietly: what could I give? Time, money, food, attention, a letter. Don't decide everything now. Just let one gift become clear enough to act on. The bell holds the time.
Saga Dawa. The fourth Tibetan month, holding the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing, when good deeds are said to multiply. Today's word.
Your line: the holy month. Today, give the one gift that became clear in the sit, and treat it as if it counted a hundred times over. Day six hundred ninety-five.

screen: `DAY 695 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YEAR TWO CLOSE: HIS OWN WORDS.`

options: walk past; the walking is the merit.

fork.reveal: pilgrims often carry stacks of small notes and give to bowl after bowl; in this month, generosity is the point of the walk.

what it means: it's a whole month, holding his birth, awakening and passing, when good deeds are said to multiply.
what a scholar hears: saga is the Tibetan name of the lunar mansion called Vishakha in Sanskrit, the root of Vesakha.

696.title: Year two close: his own words
696.hook: the truths, the path, the middle-length, the long, the short, the connected, the numbered
696.howItsDone: Many Buddhists study the discourses through chanting, reading groups and Dhamma talks, and in many monasteries and homes a favorite verse or sutta line is recited daily or kept close as a reminder.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Saga Dawa, and your line, the holy month. Did you give the gift that came clear in the sit? Today is the last day of year two. Day six hundred ninety-six.

A year ago, year two opened with a promise: the Buddha's own words. Not stories about him. Not commentary. The discourses themselves, as the early collections keep them. That's a lot of reading. Some days it was a single line. Some days it was a long walk through a long sutta. So today we stand at the lookout again, and pick up one line from each stretch of the road.
screen: `A YEAR OF HIS OWN WORDS.` → `ONE LINE FROM EACH STRETCH.`

segments.voice: First, the four noble truths. From the first sermon at the Deer Park, the whole map: there is suffering; it has a cause, which is craving; it can end; and there's a way. Then the eightfold path, factor by factor, six days each. View, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration. The line to keep: the middle way, between chasing pleasure and punishing yourself. Then the Middle-Length Sayings, read in order. From there, the raft: a teaching is like a raft you build to cross a river. You don't carry it on your head once you're across. Then the Long Discourses. From the last of the long road, the Buddha's advice in his last rains, when he was ill: be an island to yourselves, a refuge to yourselves, with the teaching as your island. Then the short books: the Sutta Nipata, the Udana, the Itivuttaka. From the Sutta Nipata, the discourse on loving-kindness: as a mother would protect her only child with her life, so keep a boundless heart toward every living being. Then the Connected and the Numbered Sayings. From the Book of Threes, near the end of that stretch: keep the pot upright, so what's poured in stays. And last, the festival year: full moons, ghosts fed, robes sewn in a day, and the passing between the sal trees, all things end. There's a Pali word for all of this: buddhavacana, the word of the Buddha. Schools of Buddhism draw the edges of that word differently. Theravada keeps the Pali canon. Mahayana schools also treasure sutras that year four will open, each in its own terms. This year we stayed with the early discourses. Not the whole forest. A good handful.
screen: `THE TRUTHS AND THE PATH.` · `THE RAFT AND THE ISLAND.` · `THE MOTHER AND THE UPRIGHT POT.` · `BUDDHAVACANA, HIS WORD.` · then, large: `YOU'VE READ HIS WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with one line from each. Settle, and let the breath find its pace. Then, slowly, one line per few breaths. Suffering has a cause, and an end. The middle way. The raft is for crossing. Be an island to yourself. A boundless heart, like a mother's. Keep the pot upright. All things end. Let each one land, then let it go. If one line stays longer than the others, let it. That might be the line for year three. The bell holds the time.
buddhavacana. The Pali and Sanskrit word for 'the word of the Buddha,' what the schools count as his teaching, closing a year spent with the truths, the path, and the early discourses. Today's word.
Your line: you've read his words. Today, write down the one line from this year that stayed, and put it where you'll see it tomorrow. Year three begins with a poet. Day six hundred ninety-six.

screen: `DAY 696 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A POET TELLS THE LIFE.`

options: carry it with you, out of gratitude.
leave it at the shore and go on.
burn it so no one else can use it.
fork.reveal: in the Middle-Length Sayings, the raft is for crossing over, not for holding onto; you leave it and walk on.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit buddhavacana: the word of the Buddha, what the schools count as his teaching.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha's words are one book.

697.title: A poet tells the life
697.hook: a poet retells the Buddha's life as a Sanskrit epic, and year three begins inside it
697.howItsDone: Buddhists come to the Buddha's life through many tellings, from the discourses and commentaries to later poems like the Buddhacarita, and in some communities these stories are read aloud, studied in classes or told at festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed year two. Your line was you've read his words. Which line did you write down, and where did you put it? Year three starts now. Day six hundred ninety-seven.

In year one this path walked through the Buddha's life the plain way: a dream, a grove, four sights on a road, a ride out at midnight. Short scenes, mostly from the old discourses and the commentaries. Then a whole year of his own words. Now the same life comes back, but in a different voice. Not a monk's report. A poet's. Somebody sat down with this story and decided it deserved everything a poet can give a king's tale: long descriptions, speeches, gardens, gods leaning in from the sky, a father who can't stop worrying. For the next stretch of days, we read that poem, one scene at a time.
screen: `THE SAME LIFE, A NEW VOICE.` → `NOT A REPORT. A POEM.`

segments.voice: The poem is called the Buddhacarita. Translators give the title as the life of the Buddha, or the acts of the Buddha. Tradition names its poet Ashvaghosha, and calls him a monk who was also a master of Sanskrit verse. This path follows an English translation by E. B. Cowell. So what changes when a life becomes a poem? First, the pace. A discourse might give the prince's comfort in a sentence. The poem lingers. It lets you hear the music in the palace and smell the gardens. Second, people speak. In the poem the king argues, a friend makes his case for pleasure, a charioteer pleads, and the prince answers each of them in his own words. You get to hear the arguments he had to get past, not only the result. Third, the sky takes part. Gods arrange what the prince sees. Doors open on their own. Some readers take these as wonders that happened. Others read them as a poet's way of saying the whole world was turning toward this moment. The poem doesn't stop to settle it. And fourth, it's still the same story. The poem keeps the beats the tradition knows: the dream, the birth, the sage, the sights, the leaving. It doesn't invent a new Buddha. It slows the old one down so you can walk beside him. That's the gift of the next weeks. Not new facts. The same steps, taken slowly, one canto at a time.
screen: `BUDDHACARITA: THE LIFE OF THE BUDDHA.` · `A POEM LINGERS.` · `PEOPLE ARGUE, AND HE ANSWERS.` · `THE SAME STEPS, TAKEN SLOWLY.` · then, large: `THE LIFE AS A POEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hear the opening slowly. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. The poem begins with a city, the old home of a sage named Kapila, a king of the Shakya clan named Shuddhodana, and his queen, Maya. That's all. A city, a king, a queen. Hold the three of them in mind the way you'd hold the first page of a long book, before anything has happened. No need to guess what comes next. Just stay with the opening, the way you'd sit at the start of a long walk. The bell holds the time.
Buddhacarita. A Sanskrit poem that tells the Buddha's life, credited by tradition to the poet Ashvaghosha. Today's word.
Your line: the life as a poem. Today, tell one ordinary moment of your day slowly, to yourself, the way a poet would, and notice what you missed the first time. Day six hundred ninety-seven.

pairs: the life, or acts, of the Buddha
the English translation this path follows

it tells them and moves on; some readers take them as events, others as a poet's picture.

fork.setup: you're a poet handed the Buddha's life, a story everyone already knows. what do you do with it?
options: change the ending so it surprises people.
slow it down and let the people in it speak.
cut it to a single page.
fork.reveal: the poem keeps the story and slows it down: gardens, music, arguments, and the prince's own answers.

original.note: Sanskrit: the Buddha's life, or his acts; the title of the poem.

trapdoor: what you thought: a biography, with dates and facts.
what it means: a long poem that retells the Buddha's life, slowing each scene and letting people speak.
what a scholar hears: kavya, the ornate Sanskrit poetry of royal courts, here turned to tell how a prince left the court.

698.title: The birth, in verse
698.hook: the queen's dream, the grove, the child who takes seven steps (Buddhacarita 1)
698.howItsDone: Some Buddhists remember the Buddha's birth at festivals such as Vesak, and in some East Asian temples images of the newborn standing with one hand raised are bathed with sweet tea or water to recall the streams from the sky.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddhacarita, and your line: the life as a poem. Did you tell one ordinary moment slowly? Today the poem reaches the birth. Day six hundred ninety-eight.

A queen lies asleep, and in her dream a white elephant enters her side. In time she asks to go out to a grove called Lumbini. The king agrees, and she goes with her women. There, in the grove, the child is born. You met these scenes in year one, told quickly, almost like a list. The poet won't hurry. He stops at the moment of birth and reaches for the old stories of India to find something to compare it with. And then he lets the newborn do something no newborn does.
screen: `A DREAM OF A WHITE ELEPHANT.` → `THE GROVE CALLED LUMBINI.` → `A NEWBORN WHO WALKS.`

segments.voice: First, the comparison. In the poem, the child comes from his mother's side, and the poet lines this up with the births of heroes and kings in older Indian legend, one born from a thigh, one from a hand, one from the head. The point isn't anatomy. It's company. The poet is saying: this birth belongs with the great births your listeners already know. Second, the steps. As soon as he is born, the poem says, the child stands and takes seven steps, firm and steady. Then he speaks. In the poem's words, given here in paraphrase, he says he is born for awakening and for the good of the world, and that this birth is his last. A newborn announcing his purpose. Third, the world answers. The poem has streams of water fall from the sky, one cool and one warm, to bathe him, and flowers come down on the grove. And fourth, the mother. It was Maya's wish that took everyone to Lumbini. Year two told that she died soon after the birth, and the poem will say so too, in the next canto. So these first steps are taken in a grove his mother chose, by a child she won't see grow. Seven steps is where the poem puts the start of the road. Every later scene in the life, the leaving, the searching, the sitting, will be more steps on it.
screen: `A BIRTH AMONG THE GREAT BIRTHS.` · `SEVEN STEPS, AND HE SPEAKS.` · `WATER FROM THE SKY, COOL AND WARM.` · `THE START OF THE ROAD.` · then, large: `SEVEN STEPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take seven slow steps. Stand up if you can, wherever you are. If you can't stand, let your hand do the walking on your knee or the table. Lift one foot, feel it move, set it down. Count one. Then the other. Count two. Seven of them, each as slow as you like, each one fully felt. When you reach seven, stop and stand still. Feel your weight on the ground. Then sit for the rest of the time, and let the seven steps settle. The bell holds the time.
The birth. In the poem: a dream, a grove, a child born from his mother's side, who stands, takes seven steps and speaks. Today's word.
Your line: seven steps. Once today, when you start something, a walk, a task, a hard conversation, take the first seven steps slowly and on purpose. Day six hundred ninety-eight.

fork.reveal: the poem compares it to legendary births, from a thigh, a hand, a head, to say this birth belongs among the great ones.

699.title: Asita's tears, in verse
699.hook: the sage weeps that he will not hear the child teach (Buddhacarita 1)
699.howItsDone: Asita's visit is told in other Buddhist texts besides this poem, and it appears in paintings and carvings of the Buddha's early life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the birth in verse, and your line: seven steps. Did you start something slowly, on purpose? Today a visitor comes to see the child. Day six hundred ninety-nine.

A palace celebrating a new baby. Then a guest nobody sent for: an old holy man, Asita, who has seen signs and come on his own. The king receives him with honor and brings out the child. Asita looks for a long time. And his eyes fill, and the tears run down. In a room like that, a holy man weeping over a newborn seems to mean only one thing. Year one met Asita in a few lines. The poem gives the scene room, and lets both men speak: a frightened father, and an old man who has to explain his tears.
screen: `A HOLY MAN NOBODY SENT FOR.` → `HE LOOKS, AND WEEPS.` → `A FATHER AFRAID.`

segments.voice: First, the king's fear. In the poem, King Shuddhodana sees the tears and trembles. He asks the sage outright: is my son's life short? Is some harm coming to him? It is the question a parent asks. Second, Asita's answer. Not for the child, he says. The child is well, and more than well. The poem has him describe what this boy will become: one who leaves the kingdom behind, wakes up, and teaches a way out of suffering for the world. In the poem's images, paraphrased here, the teaching will be like a boat that carries people across a great flood. Third, the turn. Then why weep? Because I am old, Asita says. My time is nearly over. This child will teach, and I won't be alive to hear it. The tears are for himself. He arrived at the right house, and too early in the story. Notice what he doesn't do. He doesn't resent the child. He doesn't pretend not to care. He weeps honestly, and he blesses what he won't share. And fourth, the shadow this leaves. Asita has said, in front of the king, that the boy will leave the kingdom. A father who wanted an heir has just heard he may be raising a wanderer. That sentence will sit in the palace for years. Tomorrow we see what the king does with it. Today, stay with the old man. Some people know a version of his grief: a grandparent who won't see the wedding, a founder who won't see the school finished. Asita's answer is to love it anyway, from where he stands.
screen: `IS MY SON IN DANGER?` · `NOT FOR THE CHILD.` · `I WON'T LIVE TO HEAR HIM.` · `THE BOY WILL LEAVE THE KINGDOM.` · then, large: `BORN TOO EARLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of a teacher you'll never meet. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone whose words reached you but whose face you never saw. A writer long gone. A grandparent's grandparent whose sayings got passed down. A teacher of a teacher of yours. Or someone not yet born, who will teach what you can't. Let that person sit in the room for a minute. You don't have to say anything to them. Just let there be gratitude, and a little of Asita's ache, side by side. The bell holds the time.
Asita's tears. An old sage weeps over the newborn, not from fear for the child, but because he won't live to hear him teach. Today's word.
Your line: born too early. Today, pass on one thing you know to someone who will use it long after this conversation: a recipe, a skill, a story. Day six hundred ninety-nine.

a boat across a great flood

700.title: Life in the palace
700.hook: music, gardens, the king's fear that his son will leave (Buddhacarita 2)
700.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers draw on the palace years when speaking about comfort, attachment and family love, and the story appears in temple murals and in children's classes in Buddhist communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Asita's tears, and your line: born too early. What did you do whose good you may not see? Today we go inside the palace walls. Day seven hundred.

In the evenings, music drifts down from the upper rooms of the palace. Women play and sing. The rooms open onto gardens. Down below, the kingdom is doing well; the poem says the whole land seems to flourish after the boy is born. Everything a young prince could want is brought upstairs to him. And the man who arranged all of it is afraid. It's the king. He keeps hearing an old sage's voice telling him his son will leave the kingdom. So he has decided what to do about it.

segments.voice: Year one told the palace years from the prince's side, in his own later words: three palaces, one for each season, and a life of great comfort. The poem moves the camera. It shows the palace through his father. First, the plan. The poem says plainly why the king fills the prince's days with pleasure: he remembers what Asita foretold, and he wants the boy so delighted with home that he never thinks of the forest. The music isn't only a gift. It's a strategy. Second, the details. The prince grows up in the upper rooms, among music and dancing. Out in the kingdom, the poem has the king ruling well and doing good works, as if he could hold everything steady by being good enough. Third, the family. The king arranges a marriage, to Yashodhara, and in time a son is born, Rahula. In the poem, the king is glad. A grandson is one more thread holding the prince to home. And fourth, the fear underneath. Put together, the canto is a portrait of love that can't sit still. Nothing in the palace is cruel. Every gift is real. And every gift is also a wall. The king isn't a villain in this poem. He's a father trying to write his son's story for him, with every comfort he can find. Some listeners will know that father. Some have been him. The poem doesn't mock him. It shows how hard he's holding on, and it quietly suggests the holding won't be enough. Tomorrow, something gets through.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one thing you're protected from. Settle, and breathe. Look around the life you have, gently. Maybe a parent kept a hard truth from you when you were small. Maybe your neighborhood keeps some kinds of trouble out of sight. Maybe your phone shows you only what you already like. Pick one. Don't judge the person who built the wall, and don't tear it down in your head. Just see it. Notice whether it came from love, or fear, or both. The bell holds the time.
Life in the palace. Music, gardens, a marriage and a son, all arranged by a king who fears his son will leave. Today's word.
Your line: a father's fear. Today, when someone holds on to you too tightly, see if you can find the love inside the grip before you push against it. Day seven hundred.
